First I will provide you with some of my writing, take note of the style as well of the context.

Please use this space to describe how these events have impacted you.

My family was already struggling to meet our monthly expenses. It didn't help that my dad had to close down his retail stores in the city due to the pandemic. We created two new companies that year. Due to our financial situation, my family had decided to move to Texas from New York; this would be our fifth home since I was born. We understood what this called for, but packing and unpacking are still highly time-consuming, taking away from the limited time we had.

My side business of buying and selling sought-after sneakers using automation software was also taking off at the time, so I would manage that simultaneously. I did my best to focus in class, but I admit I often worked or packed while I should've been paying attention in class.

Moving came with a whole new school where I couldn't choose my classes because I was enrolled late and wasn't even able to meet with my counselor due to covid restrictions. I juggled online classes and started new businesses back up with my dad. Covid-19 entirely shifted the way we lived from our environment and stress levels to our friends, or the lack thereof.

--

Additional Info

Many times during the last two years, I've sacrificed my focus on education to prioritize family. I've never concentrated less on school than in 2021, my junior year and a time when I was supposed to be applying for college. 

My mother was expecting my baby brother. My grandparents had just come to live with us. My elder sister was in the hospital undergoing chemotherapy as she had been diagnosed with lymphoma in March of 2021. My dad had been searching for work and found a restaurant space he would start leasing the same month of my sister's diagnosis. As the old saying goes, when it rains, it pours. 

My typical day would consist of taking online classes while replying to customers of my e-commerce business and designing content or adjusting the website for my dad's restaurant. During the lunch break, I would pack orders, prepare them to ship out, and then have my actual lunch during my next class. After classes ended around 4:30, I'd go to the hospital to check up on my sister before rushing back home to get ready to work at the restaurant until eleven at night. My grandfather, who has Parkinson's and suffers from dementia, routinely forgets where he is and runs out of the house. Since my mom could not run after him, every few days, we'd have to come back early and try to find him walking through an empty street at night. 

Obviously, this schedule left no time for studying and sometimes not even for homework. I remember staying up until 1 or 2 am after getting back to finish AP US History assignments. Since it was so impossible to retain information in class, I'd decided not to take the SAT and even skip one of three of my AP tests. I worked late nights the entire month of May, and the one day I missed work because I had an AP test in the morning was a disaster at the restaurant. 

Since I was little, I've been a straight A's, school-first student. Unfortunately, it became challenging to keep up with this mindset, but I'm happy that I learned through the obstacles and, as a result, became a more rigid and more well-rounded individual.

SMU appeals to students for a variety of reasons. Briefly describe why you are interested in attending SMU and what specific factors have led you to apply. (250-word limit)\*

SMU defines my intersection of interests and morals. 
 
One aspect that stands out is that the Cox School of Business teachers have real-world experience in the industry. An opportunity to pick their brains and bounce ideas off my professors would greatly benefit me; experience stands as the best teacher. The University also puts an emphasis on diversity and pledges that "Every Mustang Will Be Valued." Playing into that, the SMU Muslim Student Association has made efforts in raising charity for local refugees, something I can easily contribute to, given my background in the field. 
 
It's also easy to start a new student organization not already present on campus. One of my first goals would be to create a blockchain club to explore the future of the Web3 movement with my peers. The Mustangs have also partnered with the NFTU program, showing the University is open to blockchain technology. A growth environment is

My sister, who attends Boston College, recommends finding a school with a college culture I'll remember. With SMU, I get the best of both worlds, a distinct, social culture while staying close to home. Recently, I met a professor at SMU at a community service event I took part in. She encouraged me to apply and check out the campus. When I visited, there was a college football game that night, and I got to see the enthusiasm in the community—a sense of livelihood I have missed since moving from New York. 
SMU is a diverse learning environment shaped by the convergence of ideas and cultures. How will your unique experiences or background enhance the University, and how will you benefit from this community? (250-word limit)\*
I bring my passions, culture, and experiences to SMU. Sharing my journey with those around me and hearing theirs. Engaging in deep conversations about culture, religion, and ethics is nothing new to me and serves as an example to learn from. 
 
The best way to gain wisdom is from people and the environment. Being a Pakistani who comes from a background valuing family above all, I've gotten the chance to learn from the extraordinary journeys of the many who've made the voyage to America. These are my favorite stories to hear, some came to the country with little money, and even less formal education yet were successful in their endeavors through hard work and determination. 
 
An advantage I think about frequently is the exposure to various personalities as a teenager in the city of New York. Absorbing diverse concepts and ideals serves as a leg up on the majority that hasn't. Our backgrounds mold us into who we are. Moving five houses in less than 15 years doesn't sound ideal, but it made me who I am today, and looking back, I'm thankful for the situation it has put me in. 
 
I aim to continue discovering new personalities at SMU. There are numerous stories of people finding a founding team for their business by networking at their University. Tell us about a community or group to which you belong. How have you contributed to this group, and how has it benefitted you?

I owe a lot of my accomplishments to my community, without which I wouldn't merely be the person I am today. Back in New York, my family played a significant role in MANA (Memon Association of North America); this group of Memons --a minority Muslim ethnic group originating from Indian and Pakistani heritage. MANA aimed to remind community members of their South Asian roots and keep a close-knit group of familiar faces.

For my parents, when they first moved, these were the only people they interacted with outside of work. In a place like New York, it's easy to get lost in fast-paced city life and forget where you come from. Memons are known for being merchants back in South Asia, so naturally, many community members also used the gatherings to network and help each other with the business and find partners for their children. 

Everyone starts somewhere, and for graphic design, MANA was looking for someone to design a flyer for a sports event. My dad told me I should do it, but I had no idea where to begin. I used web-based software and would screenshot the result. Looking back now, using several different fonts and colors is not as artistic as it seemed back then, but every time I look back, I see progress. 

MANA got me started with graphic design, and I still use the skills I first learned today; I went from picking random website templates to making my own using Adobe Illustrator and now Figma. Just this week, I am wrapping up two freelance projects for restaurants that hired me to design their logo, menu, and promotional content, and it all started by volunteering to make a cricket event graphic. My interest in design has even brought me to web design and app design, I've started experimenting with UI, and I trust I'll make the journey just like I did with flyer design. 

I continue to make flyers for MANA even after moving to Dallas. I owe them everything I've achieved in the design space and even business-wise. I've met my best friends by going to the event and still talk to them over discord, we're all similar in our business-mindedness, and there's no doubt the community helped shape that.
--
Whether it is graphic design, business ideas, or even thinking up games to play with my cousins, I have always found ways to incorporate my concepts to improve what I'm doing. I have been writing theories in a book since I was 12 years old, including developing electric cars and blockchain technology to stop corrupt government practices. Sometimes I will take breaks just to imagine the future of our existence, our roadblocks, and our objectives for a better life. In doing so, I idealize business paths for my future that solve said problems using technology. Automation has also been a focal point for me as I am interested in problem-solving and keep an open mind to upcoming innovations.

I started in graphic design in 2016, and it has taken a significant portion of my time over the years. I visualize my ideas through digital work and incorporate my business sense to market products. I've learned Adobe Illustrator, Photoshop, Lightroom, Final Cut Pro X, and Figma, all for this purpose. Today I have designed branding language for several successful companies and continue to use digital media to my strength. My campaigns tend to go outside of the box, resulting in higher click rates due to the creative nature of the advertisements.


They say, "Curiosity killed the cat," but most don't know the end of the idiom: "and satisfaction brought it back." Satisfaction eluding to the reward that one feels once they finally find the answer they were looking for. My curiosity works similarly, sometimes not allowing me to finish my work until I have found what I am searching for, even if it may seem irrelevant at the time. I often fight with myself for needing to know how everything works; However, the pleasure it brings once I figure it out has me outweighing the cost with the benefits. 

The aspect of curiosity plays into my perfectionist persona. Everything must be top-notch, or I am left with the guilt of knowing I could have done better given a bit more time down the eternal rabbit hole. The price of curiosity does not come without its compensation, though; I believe if there is interest in a subject long enough, one will eventually become a beneficiary after investing their time and/or knowledge into a concept. 

My curiosity ranges a broad spectrum with a passion for blockchain technology, efficient marketing strategy, and human psychology, to name a few. Given a chance, I will always investigate and ask questions about a field or idea that piques my interest, and once I start, there is no end in sight. Therefore the "satisfaction" is produced when I reach a milestone in the long journey.

Self-motivation is a concept most struggle with, though I think this is the most effective type of motive. This determination has brought itself to light in my life in various ways. Tying into the endless curiosity point, my character does not rest until I believe I have achieved the highest quality given my resources. There is always somewhere I can improve. No matter how hard I've worked, if the next day was not better than the last, then I am still failing. 

While I know it is impossible to reach perfection, this does not stop me from trying. I have an infinite amount of problems to solve and concepts to learn with less time every day, so I know if I stop pushing boundaries, they will push me.

Resiliency has played a factor in my school life where an 'A' could always become an 'A+,' and my presentations would take hours because the design and transitions had to be flawless. In business, I set goals for myself at 15 years old, much higher than I expected, only to hit them in a few months. A big part of that comes from the nature of my family; we've seen ups and downs, making us immune to the worst of times and cautious at the height. My mother always says, "compare yourself only to who you were yesterday," meaning if I am not improving every day, I am falling behind.

During my time at Syosset High School, I could not become an officer of a club because of grade requirements. However, I did help out in the Investment club by raising funds after school, selling pizza. In the Entrepreneurship club, by getting four of my friends to join the club where we would meet with successful business people. 

At Independence High School:
While my time in-person at the school has been short, I have already reached out and met with the board of the National Honors Society board and am helping them create and logo for this year's merchandise using my graphic design knowledge. I enjoy this type of work as it helps me gain experience while also helping the community.

Elaborate on what you would like the college admission committee to know about you regarding personal qualities, unusual talents, academic strengths, community activities, etc

My university should know my story, the building blocks to who I am today. Having moved five homes, I have gotten a diverse look into the lives of others. Due to this, I can easily empathize with the challenges people face. In addition, I problem solve quicker than most after being exposed to multiple ways of doing a task. While a nomadic life may look stressful to most, it plays an advantage in developing my social consciousness. 

The exposure has allowed me to contribute to community efforts, such as creating a fundraiser to supply food and essentials to those suffering in the COVID-19 pandemic in New York. My friends and I arranged boxes and negotiated with retailers to provide cost-effective supplies to give out. We utilized Facebook to search for those who needed help most at the time—sometimes driving to Brooklyn, an hour drive from Long Island, just to deliver a box of food to a woman who just lost her job due to the circumstances. 

Then a monumental shift when my family moved to Dallas, but it was easy for me; I knew what had to be done and how to adapt. I was a pro at this point. Moving multiple times has allowed me to grasp a comprehensive view of the world and prepared me to adjust to my environment in the future. 

Some talents are genetic or even innate. Marketing represents this quality for me. It just seems right to me. Ever since I was young, I have been able to sell anything. At six years old, I traded my pokemon cards and snacks for what I thought was the better share of the deal. Today I run an e-commerce business selling electronics and apparel nationwide. It's just in my genes; it seems native. 
What do you consider to be your most important activity/(ies) outside of school? You may include jobs, religious activities, hobbies, and special talents. Why are these important to you? 

Experience came in many fields for me, mainly in the last two years of my life. In 2016 I volunteered to do graphic design and photography for a local community my family was involved in. Their goal was to involve more youth members using digital media. 

The only problem was, I had no prior experience. I used web-based programs for the flyer designs, and I would use my sister's Nikon camera to shoot pictures for the photography. Later on, I'd go on to explore the depths of how I can use digital media.2 I learned photography, video editing, and some graphic design in just a couple of weeks. I was eager to learn, and designing seemed to come easily with my interest in tech. 

Little did I know this volunteering changed everything for me. It took years to grasp some design and video editing concepts, many of which I don't even know today, but most beneficial was the start. A few years later, I was hired for some baking company to make Instagram posts. I would charge $20 for each. Looking back at it, I realize my prices were extremely low for the quality of work. 

During the same time, my friend had told me about the profitable business of reselling sneakers. I tried that and started using my graphic design experience to create high-ranking eBay listings for what I was selling. I didn't think much of it for some time...

Then the world was hit with the COVID-19 pandemic. I started to help my dad shift his business because his sole source of income, physical cell phone stores, had to be shut down due to the state mandate. My dad and I would build a wholesale brand in March of 2020 to make an income. I would also explore resale opportunities on the side, separately, that I would start saving up and investing in. From some birthday money I was saving up for three years, I had managed to buy shoes, toys, and other limited, high-profit items. 

When we moved to Texas, I had some capital left after liquidating my small stock in New York. I made choices based on what we learned in class, and I would buy popular children's toys and games to prepare for the holiday season when supply would be low, but demand would skyrocket. The market was low on stock due to shipping difficulties regarding the pandemic, increasing the already high holiday premiums leading to my first 1,000 orders, all while attending virtual classes from my laptop. I would write my essays early in the morning to have enough time to package shipments for the afternoon. 


Which high school teacher/class has impacted you most, and why/how?

In 10th grade, I took a College Marketing Class; this would be my first College Level course, earning me six credits by the end of the school year. The class would serve my interests and introduce new strategies to me. 

Through the course, I gained the opportunity to be selected for a marketing and design competition—a perfect blend of my skills. We were posed with creating a logo and rebranding strategy for an old Italian restaurant looking to open itself up to a younger crowd. Using my graphic design experience and my newly found marketing strategies, I worked a month on the poster board and elements to present. I would stay after school and come early to create what I thought was my best work at the time. 

I ended up getting 2nd place out of the 32 contestants that day. The only weakness in my display was my presenting skills; I had focused too much on the graphics and board aesthetics that I forgot to review the delivery. I'd be super observant in class for the rest of the course to up my presentation ability. I felt so defeated that I watched hours of presenters on YouTube for the next few months. I've watched TED Talks on every topic. Today, I am a confident presenter and can establish my presence acting as a magnet to watch and absorb.

In what ways are you more prepared to live independently than you were two years ago?

For most of last year, I already felt I was living independently. My sister was home from Boston College after getting diagnosed with Leukemia. My mother was expecting my younger brother. Meanwhile, my dad would search for work, and my little sister would be in school until 3:30. With my virtual classes in session, I would be responsible for making my meals and making enough for my mom and sisters. I realized afterward that the experience helped a lot with my time management skills, even experimenting by getting up earlier to give myself a head start on the day. I downloaded the Walmart+ app, so instead of going to the grocery store when my mom wasn't feeling well, we could just order groceries digitally, saving a lot of time and energy.

What do you hope to accomplish in the future? What are your post-graduate plans?

Have you ever heard of the 'Zone of Genius'? Gay Hendricks wrote about the concept in his book The Big Leap. Simply put, it is the point where all your skills and your 'innate genius' meet. The zone is what is most seems most effortless for you and difficult for the majority. To bring it to its potential, we must practice our natural talent and blend it with our passions. For me, that is Graphic Design and Marketing paired with my interest in blockchain technology. Along with some friends, I have already started building a project utilizing the technology, and I have so many ideas on how to implement it into everyone's daily life. 

Blockchain is my future because it is ultimately humanity's future. The technology is our only hope to introduce a transparent commerce system when the people in power prefer to hide their shady dealings. It solves the problem of corruption and resolves some of the power of giant corporations. Blockchain technology can't be stopped, and nor can I.

The only thing I know for certain is that blockchain will be involved in my future; the rest is flexible. Given the adaptable nature I eluded earlier, I am willing to go where life takes me.

My GPA would look better if I did not engage in multiple out-of-school activities last year. I would work on my e-commerce business for a significant portion of the day, leaving less time for school work and studying. The only day I took off was the day of my AP test. Had I portioned the time out for studying instead of working, I would see the results in my favor. However, I decided on my future as I believe the experience I gained combats a few percentage points. 

The same goes for my SAT, I probably should have studied when I was working, but I did not. I took my first SAT this year with no PSAT before. Decisions were made; I can't tell if they were good ones until the future.

As for my Freshman and Sophomore grades, I am pretty satisfied knowing the rigorous courses offered there. I never missed honor roll any quarter, and knowing how competitive the school was, it felt like an outstanding achievement. The classes were challenging, and I knew no one with a perfect GPA there. 

However, I learned that Frisco School District often allows retests on every exam until a student reaches 100% and uses other tactics such as 'waterfalling' to ensure no student fails. Therefore my GPA will be lower than most of the others because my former school did not allow such practices. Although this is the case, I won't let it worry me as it will push me harder to come out on top.

Q. What is “Pay with Miles/Mix Miles and Cash”?
A. “Pay with Miles” (PwM)/Mix Miles with Cash is the project enabling KrisFlyer (KF) members to use their KF miles as payment or partial payment of their commercial tickets and selected ancillaries on singaporeair.com (SAA).
Q. How will this payment method benefits KF members?
A, Members will be able to use this payment option for all commercial booking classes available on SAA, which means that they will have access to all available seats on all flights operated by SIA. Members will also have control over the number of miles they want to use, as long as it is more than the minimum required. Members will have more opportunities to use their miles before expiry. 
Q. What is the minimum number of miles required to pay for a commercial ticket?
A. A minimum of approximately 1050 KF miles is required per transaction (i.e., per PNR). This minimum may vary as the conversion rate from SGD to KF miles is subject to change upon review. For information only: The conversion rate is stored as SGD 1: 105 KF miles, hence the KF miles deducted for such a transaction will always be in multiples of 105 miles.
Q. Is there a maximum number of miles which is allowed to be used?
A. No, members can pay up to 100% of the commercial ticket using miles (inclusive of airport taxes and surcharges).
Q. If members do not have enough miles, can they purchase miles to pay for tickets?
A. No, purchase of miles is only available when redeeming award tickets or flight upgrades.
Q. Will members be able to use their miles to pay for taxes and surcharges on their commercial tickets?
A. Yes, members will be able to use their miles to pay for airport taxes and surcharges of their commercial tickets bought on SAA. 
In other words, the entire commercial ticket can be paid for with miles.
Q. Can members use their miles to pay for the tickets of their friends and family?
A. Members can use their miles to pay for the commercial tickets of their nominees (RGN) only. Members can nominate up to a maximum of 5 RGNs. Nominees can be added at any time. However, once added, these RGNs cannot be removed or changed for a period of 6 months and a fee is applicable.
Q. Can members use their miles to pay for flights on another airline?
A. No, members are only able to use their miles for SIA operated flights. If members were to purchase an itinerary on SAA which includes a codeshare flight operated by another airline, they would also be unable to use KF miles to pay for the SIA operated flight within that itinerary.
Q. Can members use KF miles to pay for a booking made through a travel agent?
A. No, the KF miles payment option is only available for KF members via SAA. 
Q. For transactions in foreign currencies, would the cash component be rounded up or down? Would it be rounded off to the nearest dollar?
A. Itineraries originating from outside Singapore will be priced in local currencies (as per current SAA logic), and the local fares will be converted to SGD (based on the IATA rounding logic) before being converted to KF miles. 
Q. What is the SGD to miles conversion rate?
A. The current conversion rate is SGD1per 105 KF miles. This rate will be reviewed periodically and is subject to change. 
Q. Will the SGD to miles conversion rate be made known to members?
A. The conversion rate will not be explicitly made known to members on SAA (both on the content pages and the booking flow). However, if members were to enquire about the conversion rate or about the monetary value of the miles in their accounts, you can share that the conversion rate is currently SGD1 per 105 KF miles. Members can then work out the value of their miles and the amount they wish to use. Please note that this conversion rate will be reviewed periodically and is subject to change. 
Q. Will members be able to accrue PPS Value, Elite miles and KF miles if they use their miles as payment for their commercial ticket?
A. Yes, KrisFlyer and Elite miles will be earned, in proportion to the fare (excluding airport taxes) paid using credit/debit card if the fare is mileage accruable. The PPS Value accrued will similarly be derived from the proportion paid using credit/debit card. The current conditions for accruing and calculating PPS Value still apply. As a result of this logic, the KF miles used to pay for a transaction will first be used to offset all the airport taxes of all the tickets before being used to offset the fare and fuel surcharges of the tickets. Please note that Elite miles and KF miles accrued on tickets that are partially paid for using KF miles can only be accrued to KF account. The miles accrued on such tickets cannot be parked with any other OFFPs.
Q. Will members be able to opt to accrue miles for other KF members before themselves?
A. No, we have optimized the accruals to benefit the principal member (the member who has used his/her miles to purchase the tickets). Members will not be able to adjust this logic.
Q. Can members accrue miles to OFFP accounts?
A. No, the miles earned from a commercial ticket paid for with KF miles can only be credited to their KF accounts. 
Q. Are these tickets subject to any special conditions?
A. Yes, commercial tickets paid for with KF miles are strictly non-endorsable, even if the purchased fare is one which is fully endorsable. Other than that, the prevailing commercial conditions associated with the fare paid will be applicable.
Q. Are redemption upgrades allowed for tickets that are paid for with KF miles?
A. Yes, redemption upgrades are allowed for tickets that are paid for with KF miles as long as the commercial fare is in an upgradeable booking class.
Q. Will members be able to make changes to their tickets paid for with KF miles on SAA?
A. For flight or itinerary changes, members will have to contact their local SIA office or call centres. Any additional collection resulting from these changes can only be paid for using credit card/debit card/cash. Fare conditions will apply. Members will be able to submit their request for booking changes via SAA which will be routed offline for handling. These requests will be routed based on the POS for that transaction. For seat and meal requests, members will be able to self-service on SAA. 
Q. Can a ticket paid for with KF miles be issued by AROs/call centres?
A. Offline assistance is to be provided to the passenger for exceptional handling only.
Q. How do we service a customer when SAA is down?
A. This payment feature is only available on SAA. As a result, if SAA is down, KF miles will not be an available payment option at that time. Member will be able to continue to complete the transaction offline, but payment must be made using credit/debit card. 
Q. Will members be able to go back onto SAA to do seat and meal requests after their bookings are reissued offline?
A. Yes, as per all commercial tickets, members can make seat and meal requests on SAA for their tickets paid for with KF miles even if they have been reissued offline by AROs/call centres. 
Q. Can tickets paid for with KF miles be refunded on SAA?
A. Yes, as per all other commercial tickets, tickets paid for with KF miles can be submitted for refunds on SAA if the tickets are completely unflown and have not been reissued. The maximum amount paid using credit/debit card will be refunded to members first (not exceeding the original amount paid using credit/debit card). The balance will then be refunded accordingly in miles. KF miles that have expired, will not be refunded.
Q. How will the refund be handled for cancellations of a ticket paid for with miles?
A. If refunds are applicable, then the maximum possible amount of the fare paid using credit/debit card (but not more than the original amount paid using credit/debit card) will be refunded first. The remaining refund amount, if any, will be returned in equivalent miles. In other words, we will always refund the “cash” amount first (not exceeding the original amount paid using credit/debit card), before refunding the KF miles. This logic also applies to the refund of residual value when a ticket is reissued from a higher fare to a lower fare. KF miles that have expired, will not be refunded.
Q. Will residual miles be refunded for reissuance from higher fares to lower fares?
A. For a booking change from a higher fare to a lower fare, the refund logic will apply to the residual value. In other words, we will always refund the “cash” amount first (not exceeding the original amount paid using credit/debit card). Any balance refund amount will then be refunded in miles. KF miles that have expired will not be refunded.
Q. What happens if some miles used to pay for the flight have already expired at the point of refund?
A. The expired miles will not be refunded. Only miles which have not expired can be refunded. Any applicable fees and charges associated with the refund will be deducted from the oldest miles used for the ticket. I.e., Expired miles will be used to deduct such charges first. 
Q. How can we verify whether the miles the member used to pay for the flight have already expired?
A. Information on the expiry of the miles used for tickets is available in the transaction record in MARMS. Alternatively, once the refund mask has been created in Altea, the information is displayed as a response from MARMS. Members will also be advised of this if they submit their tickets for refund on SAA. 
Q. How can members submit their tickets paid for with miles for refund?
A. Members can either submit their tickets for refund on SAA or they may contact their nearest SIA office to do so. For tickets submitted for refund offline, these tickets must be refunded by the original issue station. 
Q. When will the miles be credited back to members’ accounts when they submit their tickets paid for with miles for refund?
A. The miles will be returned to members’ account immediately once the refund is successfully completed. 
Q. If members have purchased a commercial ticket paid fully with credit/debit card, will they be able to use miles to pay for any additional collection resulting from a reissuance?
A. No, this new payment option is only available on SAA for new ticket issuance. 
Q. Will members be able to use their miles to pay for any other services available on SAA?
A. No, KF miles are only available as a payment method for commercial tickets. We are working on increasing the list of SIA services members can use their KF miles to pay for. 
Q. Can members use their miles to pay for the taxes and surcharges on their redemption award tickets?
A. No, members can only use their miles to pay for commercial bookings (including taxes and surcharges) made on SAA. We are working on enabling members to pay for taxes and surcharges on their redemption tickets in the next phase of development.
Q. When can members use their KF miles to pay for taxes and surcharges on their redemption tickets or for any other SIA services?
A. We are working on enabling members to use their miles to pay for (i) taxes and surcharges on their redemption tickets and (ii) other SIA services. This will be in the next phase of development.
Q. Will OFFP members (e.g., LH Miles & More member using LH miles) be able to use their own miles from their respective FFP programmes if they are not KF members?
A. No, only KF miles can be used for this new payment option. Hence, only KF members (who accrue KF miles) will be able to use this payment option. 
Q. Can member continue to use their KF miles to redeem Saver, Standard and Full Award tickets?
A. Yes, we will continue to maintain the current redemption options for members. This is an additional programme feature which will increase the number of options for members to make use of their miles.
Q. Is it better to use KF miles to pay for a commercial ticket or redeem an award ticket?
A. The number of miles required to pay for a commercial ticket depends on the fares available at the time of purchase. Customers are advised to check the mileage requirement for both the commercial ticket and the Award redemption, as well as to consider the applicable fare conditions before deciding which ticket type is more suitable for their purpose.
Q. Will members be able to pay for an infant ticket with miles?
A. Currently, infant nominees are not available in the dropdown list on SAA. However, once this feature is made available on the commercial booking flow, members will be able to pay for their infant tickets with miles.
Q. Will members be able to make a booking for himself and/or his nominees and other passengers who are not his nominees?
A. Yes, however, members will only be able to use their miles to pay for the tickets for themselves and their nominees. They will have pay for the tickets of any other passengers using credit/debit card. 
Q. For tickets paid for with miles with itineraries starting from MI destinations, will MI be able to service (reissue/revalidate/refund) these tickets?
A. No, as these tickets involve the collection of miles, they will have to be routed to SQ for handling. This is similar to the handling of redemption tickets. 
Q. When voiding a reissue of a ticket originally paid for with miles, the FOP for the reissue must be deleted before attempting another reissue. Why is this so?
A. MARMs will return an approval code for all reissue ticket and this approval code is appended into the FOP field. When the reissue ticket is voided, a void message is sent to MARMs and the approval code will be invalidated by MARMS. Hence, if the FOP is not deleted, Altea will use the same approval code to issue the new ticket and this new ticket number will not be updated by MARMS. Subsequent servicing such as reissue or refund will fail since MARMS has no record of this new ticket.
Q. Why is voiding the refund of a ticket originally paid for with miles not allowed even when sales report is not closed yet?
A. Like a redemption ticket, Altea does not send any void message to MARMs for voiding of a refund record for tickets originally paid with miles. Hence, MARMs will not be aware that the refund is voided and subsequent attempt to refund the ET will fail.
Q. How can members submit their tickets paid for with miles for refund?
A. Members can either submit their tickets for refund on SAA or they may contact their nearest SIA office to do so. For tickets submitted for refund offline, these tickets must be refunded by the original issue station. 
Q. Why must refund of tickets, which has been paid with miles, always be refunded by original issue station?
A. If refund is done by a different station, BBR will be used to convert refundable amount to the refund station currency. However, MARMS only stores IATA exchange rate. Hence, there is a possibility that the converted amount using BBR may be higher that the converted rate by MARMS, thus resulting in refund failure. 
Q. For tickets paid for with miles, cover refund is permitted for a flown ticket but not an already refunded ticket. Why is this so?
A. Altea will make a call to MARMs for all refund of tickets which has been paid for with miles. MARMs will have a record that the ticket is already refunded, hence further refund will not be allowed. MARMS has no record that the ticket is flown, hence cover refund is still allowed for flown ticket.
Q. Zero refund is not allowed for tickets paid for with miles. Why is this so?
A. MARMS expects to receive the FOP details for tickets paid for with miles in the refund message from Altea. However, there is no FOP for zero refund, hence zero refund is not allowed for ticket, which has been paid with miles. For reissue of tickets paid for with miles, only cash is allowed if additional fare is required. Why is FQTR still a mandatory element for such reissues and also reissue without adc as well? MARMS need the FQTR number from Altea in order to create the MARMs record for the reissue transaction.
Q. If the member wants to use 100% of the miles for his own ticket only, can he select "Not a nominee" in the passenger details and manually type in his RGN's details?
A. The logic for accruals has been defaulted to always favour the principal member. The principal member will always accrue full miles before the nominee (also a KF member) accrues any miles. In the event the principal member would like to use miles to pay for his own ticket and not his nominee, he may choose not to select his nominee from the dropdown list. Instead, he could choose 'Not a nominee' and enter the 2nd pax details manually, he will not be able to use miles for this 2nd pax. In this case, the principal member will get either partial/no accrual while pax 2 will get full accrual. 
Q. Why a residual value eMD, that is issued against a ticket paid for with miles, cannot be reissued into another ET or eMD? 
A. Such reissue is not in scope for phase 1. MARMs will return an error message to Altea and reissue will fail. Hence, the eMD must be submitted for refund. This will be reviewed by LMD in phase 2.

# This class represents arbitrary byte select compression algorithms.
# An algorithm is represented as a graph where a travesal from source to 
# sink is a valid encoding of some input data. An encoding is composed of 
# a flexible byte dictionary, a fixed byte dictionary, and some metadata 
# which can be used to reconstruct the original data from bytes in the
# dictionaries and from constants.
#
# The vertices of the graph are of two main types: choice and assignment. 
# A choice vertex is used only for choosing between two or more possible 
# encdings. The edges in a traversal outgoing from choice vertices determine 
# the metadata required to encode a given tarversal.
# An assignment vertex is used to assert that a value in the input has been
# stored in one of the dictionaries or matches a predetermined constant.
#
# There are four types of assignment vertices, and they are parameterized by 
# integer tuple properties:
# (1) Constant Assignment
# A vertex with property (i, c) which asserts that the byte at index i in
# the input data is equal to a constant c.
# (2) Flexible Dictionary Store Assignment
# A vertex with property (i) which asserts that the byte at index i in the
# input data was stored in the first free byte of the flexible dictionary.
# (3) Flexible Dictionary Reference Assignment
# A vertex with property (i0, i1) which asserts that the byte at i0 was
# previously stored in the flexible dictionary and matches the value at 
# i1 in the input data.
# (4) Fixed Dictionary Assignment
# A vertex with property (i, d) which asserts that the byte at index i in 
# the input matches the value at index d of the fixed dictionary or was
# stored at index d if no value is present.

from math import log2, ceil

class Algo(): 
 class Vertex():
 def \_\_init\_\_(self):
 self.in\_edges = []
 self.out\_edges = []
 self.protected = False

 def \_\_str\_\_(self):
 retval = "\n\tID: " + str(id(self)) + "\n"
 retval += "\tVertex type: " + str(type(self)) + "\n"
 try:
 retval += "\tProperty: " + str(self.property) + "\n"
 except: pass
 retval += "\tProtected: " + str(self.protected) + "\n"
 retval += "\tParents: "
 for e in self.in\_edges:
 retval += str(id(e.source)) + " "
 retval += "\n\tChildren: "
 for e in self.out\_edges:
 retval += str(id(e.target)) + " "
 return retval

 class Edge():
 def \_\_init\_\_(self, source, target):
 self.source = source
 self.target = target
 self.protected = False

 class ChoiceVertex(Vertex):
 def \_\_init\_\_(self):
 super().\_\_init\_\_()
 self.bottleneck = False

 class AssignmentVertex(Vertex):
 def \_\_init\_\_(self, property):
 super().\_\_init\_\_()
 self.property = property

 class ConstantAssignmentVertex(AssignmentVertex):
 def \_\_init\_\_(self, index, value):
 assert isinstance(index, int)
 assert isinstance(value, int)
 super().\_\_init\_\_((index, value))

 class FlexibleStoreAssignmentVertex(AssignmentVertex):
 def \_\_init\_\_(self, index):
 assert isinstance(index, int)
 super().\_\_init\_\_((index,))

 class FlexibleReferenceAssignmentVertex(AssignmentVertex):
 def \_\_init\_\_(self, index, reference):
 assert isinstance(index, int)
 assert isinstance(reference, int)
 super().\_\_init\_\_((index, reference))

 class FixedAssignmentVertex(AssignmentVertex):
 def \_\_init\_\_(self, index, dictionary\_index):
 assert isinstance(index, int)
 assert isinstance(dictionary\_index, int)
 super().\_\_init\_\_((index, dictionary\_index))

 def \_\_init\_\_(self, algoConfig=None, algo=None):
 self.verbose = algoConfig["verbose"]
 self.debug = algoConfig["debug"]

 if algo is None:
 self.constructor(algoConfig)
 else:
 self.copy\_constructor(algo)

 def constructor(self, algoConfig):
 assert algoConfig is not None

 blockSize = algoConfig["block-size"]
 bottleneckStep = algoConfig["bottleneck-step"]

 self.blockSize = blockSize
 self.source = self.ChoiceVertex()
 self.sink = self.ChoiceVertex()
 self.vertices = [self.source, self.sink]
 self.edges = []

 if algoConfig["init-algo"]["name"] == "BSI":
 self.add\_bsi(algoConfig["init-algo"])
 else:
 self.add\_default()

 def add\_default(self):
 # Initialize the algorithm to assign one fixed dictionary byte to each
 # input byte. This corresponds to no compression
 prevVertex = self.source
 for i in range(self.blockSize):
 #v = self.add\_vertex(self.FixedAssignmentVertex(i, i), prevVertex)
 v = self.add\_vertex(self.FlexibleStoreAssignmentVertex(i), prevVertex)
 # Add intermediate choice vertices to allow for additions to the 
 # graph even while everything added in \_\_init\_\_ is protected
 if i < self.blockSize - 1:
 v = self.add\_vertex(self.ChoiceVertex(), v)
 if i % bottleneckStep == 0:
 v.bottleneck = True
 prevVertex = v
 e = self.add\_edge(prevVertex, self.sink)
 # Don't allow removal of the this path.
 for v in self.vertices: v.protected = True
 for e in self.edges: e.protected = True

 self.check\_graph()

 def copy\_constructor(self, algo):
 self.blockSize = algo.blockSize

 self.vertices = []
 self.edges = []

 # Copy all vertices, storing the mapping from old to new vertices
 vertexMap = {}
 for v in algo.vertices:
 try:
 vertexMap[v] = self.add\_vertex(type(v)(\*v.property))
 except:
 vertexMap[v] = self.add\_vertex(type(v)())
 vertexMap[v].protected = v.protected
 try:
 vertexMap[v].bottleneck = v.bottleneck
 except: pass

 # Copy all edges
 edgeMap = {}
 for e in algo.edges:
 edgeMap[e] = self.Edge(vertexMap[e.source], vertexMap[e.target])
 edgeMap[e].protected = e.protected
 self.edges.append(edgeMap[e])

 # Add the edges to the vertices in the same order as the original
 for v in algo.vertices:
 for e in v.in\_edges:
 vertexMap[v].in\_edges.append(edgeMap[e])
 for e in v.out\_edges:
 vertexMap[v].out\_edges.append(edgeMap[e])

 # Set the source and sink
 self.source = vertexMap[algo.source]
 self.sink = vertexMap[algo.sink]

 self.check\_graph()

 def add\_vertex(self, vertex, prevVertex=None, nextVertex=None, edgeIndex=0):
 self.log("Adding vertex " + str(id(vertex)), 2)
 self.vertices.append(vertex)
 if prevVertex is not None:
 self.add\_edge(prevVertex, vertex, edgeIndex)
 if nextVertex is not None:
 self.add\_edge(vertex, nextVertex, edgeIndex)
 return vertex

 def remove\_vertex(self, vertex):
 if vertex.protected: return
 if vertex not in self.vertices: return

 self.log("Removing vertex " + str(vertex), 1)

 self.vertices.remove(vertex)

 edges = vertex.in\_edges + vertex.out\_edges
 for e in edges:
 self.remove\_edge(e)

 def cleanup\_vertex(self, vertex):
 if vertex.protected: return
 # Remove the vertex if it not connected to the source or sink
 if len(vertex.out\_edges) == 0 or len(vertex.in\_edges) == 0:
 self.remove\_vertex(vertex)
 # Remove the vertex and connect the grandparents to the target
 # if the source is a ChoiceVertex with only one outgoing edge
 elif isinstance(vertex, self.ChoiceVertex) and \
 len(vertex.out\_edges) == 1 and not vertex.protected:
 # Perform the bypass by hand to avoid recursive calls to cleanup
 target = vertex.out\_edges[0].target
 for e in vertex.in\_edges:
 e.target = target
 target.in\_edges.append(e)
 target.in\_edges.remove(vertex.out\_edges[0])
 self.edges.remove(vertex.out\_edges[0])
 self.vertices.remove(vertex)

 def add\_edge(self, source, target, edgeIndex=-1):
 self.log("Adding edge from " + str(id(source)) + " to " + str(id(target)), 2)

 assert source != target

 self.edges.append(self.Edge(source, target))
 if edgeIndex != -1:
 source.out\_edges.insert(edgeIndex, self.edges[-1])
 target.in\_edges.insert(edgeIndex, self.edges[-1])
 else:
 source.out\_edges.append(self.edges[-1])
 target.in\_edges.append(self.edges[-1])
 return self.edges[-1]
 def remove\_edge(self, edge):
 if edge.protected: return
 if edge not in self.edges: return

 self.log("Removing edge " + str(id(edge)) + " from " + str(id(edge.source)) + " to " + str(id(edge.target)), 1)

 self.edges.remove(edge)

 edge.source.out\_edges.remove(edge)
 edge.target.in\_edges.remove(edge)
 
 self.cleanup\_vertex(edge.source)
 self.cleanup\_vertex(edge.target)

 def add\_bsi(self, initConfig): 

 createDeltaBottlenecks = initConfig["create-delta-bottlenecks"]
 createWordBottlenecks = initConfig["create-word-bottlenecks"]

 # Define tuples in the form 
 # ((base bytes, num bases), (delta bytes, num deltas))
 # where base bytes is the number of bytes used to store the base
 # and num bases is the number of bases that can be stored in the base 
 # section of the byte dictionry. Similarly for deltas.
 base\_deltas = [((8, 3), (4, 4))] #, 
 #((8, 3), (2, 6)), 
 #((4, 8), (2, 6)),
 #((4, 6), (1, 10))]

 # Add the corresponding paths to the graph for each tuple, also
 # allowing for constant zeroes in the base and delta sections
 for base, delta in base\_deltas:

 base\_bytes, num\_bases = base
 delta\_bytes, num\_deltas = delta
 delta\_offset = num\_bases \* (base\_bytes-delta\_bytes)

 self.log("Adding encodings for base\_bytes=%d, num\_bases=%d, delta\_bytes=%d, num\_deltas=%d" % (base\_bytes, num\_bases, delta\_bytes, num\_deltas), 1)

 curWord = self.source
 for wordStart in range(0, self.blockSize, base\_bytes):
 self.log("Adding word at offset %d" % wordStart, 1)
 # instantiate the choice vertex for the next word where we will
 # terminate all paths encoding the current word
 if wordStart < self.blockSize - base\_bytes:
 nextWord = self.ChoiceVertex()
 self.add\_vertex(nextWord)
 if createWordBottlenecks:
 nextWord.bottleneck = True
 else: 
 nextWord = self.sink

 # Add the path for the constant zero base
 prevVertex = curWord
 for b in range(wordStart, wordStart + base\_bytes):
 self.log("Adding constant zero base at byte " + str(b), 1)
 v = self.ConstantAssignmentVertex(b, 0)
 self.add\_vertex(v, prevVertex)
 prevVertex = v
 self.add\_edge(prevVertex, nextWord)
 
 # Add the paths for storing the deltas which
 # we will point to from the base section
 deltaChoices = self.ChoiceVertex()
 self.add\_vertex(deltaChoices)
 if createDeltaBottlenecks:
 deltaChoices.bottleneck = True
 for j in range(min(num\_deltas, int(wordStart/base\_bytes) + 1)):
 prevVertexDelta = deltaChoices
 deltaStart = wordStart + base\_bytes - delta\_bytes
 for b2 in range(deltaStart, deltaStart + delta\_bytes):
 deltaIndex = delta\_offset + j\*delta\_bytes + b2 - deltaStart
 self.log("Adding delta pointer {}->{}".format(b2, deltaIndex), 1)
 v = self.FixedAssignmentVertex(b2, deltaIndex)
 self.add\_vertex(v, prevVertexDelta)
 prevVertexDelta = v
 self.add\_edge(prevVertexDelta, nextWord)

 # Add the paths for storing the base
 for i in range(min(num\_bases, int(wordStart/base\_bytes) + 1)):
 prevVertex = curWord
 for b1 in range(wordStart, wordStart + base\_bytes - delta\_bytes):
 baseIndex = i\*(base\_bytes-delta\_bytes) + b1 - wordStart
 self.log("Adding base pointer {}->{}".format(b1, baseIndex), 1)
 v = self.FixedAssignmentVertex(b1, baseIndex)
 self.add\_vertex(v, prevVertex)
 prevVertex = v
 # Add an edge to the previously created delta paths
 self.add\_edge(prevVertex, deltaChoices)

 curWord = nextWord

 self.check\_graph()

 # This method adds the all zero encoding with top priority

 prevVertex = v
 self.add\_edge(prevVertex, self.sink)

 def compress(self, data):
 # This method compresses the data using the algorithm.
 # The data must be a list of bytes.
 assert(len(data) == self.blockSize)

 #print(data)

 fixedDictValues = [None] \* self.blockSize
 flexDictIndices = []

 # Traverse the graph depth first trying to reach the sink.
 def traverse(vertex, path):
 if vertex == self.sink:
 return path
 if isinstance(vertex, self.ChoiceVertex):
 for edge in vertex.out\_edges:
 result = traverse(edge.target, path)
 if result is not None:
 path.insert(0, (edge, len(vertex.out\_edges)))
 return result
 elif isinstance(vertex, self.ConstantAssignmentVertex):

 return traverse(vertex.out\_edges[0].target, path)
 elif isinstance(vertex, self.FlexibleStoreAssignmentVertex):
 flexDictIndices.append(vertex.property[0])
 result = traverse(vertex.out\_edges[0].target, path)

Xiang Lisa Li
Stanford University
xlisali@stanford.edu
Percy Liang
Stanford University
pliang@cs.stanford.edu
Abstract
Fine-tuning is the de facto way to leverage
large pretrained language models to perform
downstream tasks. However, it modifies all
the language model parameters and therefore
necessitates storing a full copy for each task.
In this paper, we propose prefix-tuning, a
lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for natural language generation tasks, which keeps
language model parameters frozen, but optimizes a small continuous task-specific vector
(called the prefix). Prefix-tuning draws inspiration from prompting, allowing subsequent tokens to attend to this prefix as if it were “virtual tokens”. We apply prefix-tuning to GPT-2
for table-to-text generation and to BART for
summarization. We find that by learning only
0.1% of the parameters, prefix-tuning obtains
comparable performance in the full data setting, outperforms fine-tuning in low-data settings, and extrapolates better to examples with
topics unseen during training.
1 Introduction
Fine-tuning is the prevalent paradigm for using
large pretrained language models (LMs) (Radford
et al., 2019; Devlin et al., 2019) to perform downstream tasks (e.g., summarization), but it requires
updating and storing all the parameters of the LM.
Consequently, to build and deploy NLP systems
that rely on large pretrained LMs, one currently
needs to store a modified copy of the LM parameters for each task. This can be prohibitively expensive, given the large size of current LMs; for example, GPT-2 has 774M parameters (Radford et al.,
2019) and GPT-3 has 175B parameters (Brown
et al., 2020).
A natural approach to this problem is lightweight
fine-tuning, which freezes most of the pretrained
parameters and augments the model with small
trainable modules. For example, adapter-tuning
Figure 1: Fine-tuning (top) updates all Transformer
parameters (the red Transformer box) and requires storing a full model copy for each task. We propose
prefix-tuning (bottom), which freezes the Transformer
parameters and only optimizes the prefix (the red prefix blocks). Consequently, we only need to store the
prefix for each task, making prefix-tuning modular and
space-efficient. Note that each vertical block denote
transformer activations at one time step.
(Rebuffi et al., 2017; Houlsby et al., 2019) inserts
additional task-specific layers between the layers
of pretrained language models. Adapter-tuning
has promising performance on natural language
understanding and generation benchmarks, attaining comparable performance with fine-tuning while
adding only around 2-4% task-specific parameters
(Houlsby et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2020).
On the extreme end, GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020)
can be deployed without any task-specific tuning.
Instead, users prepend a natural language task instruction (e.g., TL;DR for summarization) and a
few examples to the task input; then generate the
output from the LM. This approach is known as
in-context learning or prompting.
In this paper, we propose prefix-tuning, a
lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for natural language generation (NLG) tasks, inspired by prompting. Consider the task of generating a textual dearXiv:2101.00190v1 [cs.CL] 1 Jan 2021
scription of a data table, as shown in Figure 1,
where the task input is a linearized table (e.g.,
“name: Starbucks | type: coffee shop”) and the output is a textual description (e.g., “Starbucks serves
coffee.”). Prefix-tuning prepends a sequence of
continuous task-specific vectors to the input, which
we call a prefix, depicted by red blocks in Figure 1
(bottom). For subsequent tokens, the Transformer
can attend to the prefix as if it were a sequence of
“virtual tokens”, but unlike prompting, the prefix
consists entirely of free parameters which do not
correspond to real tokens. In contrast to fine-tuning
in Figure 1 (top), which updates all Transformer
parameters and thus requires storing a tuned copy
of the model for each task, prefix-tuning only optimizes the prefix. Consequently, we only need
to store one copy of the large Transformer and a
learned task-specific prefix, yielding a very small
overhead for each additional task (e.g., 250K parameters for table-to-text).
In contrast to fine-tuning, prefix-tuning is modular: we train an upstream prefix which steers a
downstream LM, which remains unmodified. Thus,
a single LM can support many tasks at once. In
the context of personalization where the tasks correspond to different users (Shokri and Shmatikov,
2015; McMahan et al., 2016), we could have a separate prefix for each user trained only on that user’s
data, thereby avoiding data cross-contamination.
Moreover, the prefix-based architecture enables us
to even process examples from multiple users/tasks
in a single batch, something that is not possible
with other lightweight fine-tuning approaches.
We evaluate prefix-tuning on table-to-text generation using GPT-2 and abstractive summarization using BART. In terms of storage, prefix-tuning
stores 1000x fewer parameters than fine-tuning. In
terms of performance when trained on full datasets,
prefix-tuning and fine-tuning are comparable for
table-to-text (§6.1), while prefix-tuning suffers a
small degradation for summarization (§6.2). In lowdata settings, prefix-tuning on average outperforms
fine-tuning on both tasks (§6.3). Prefix-tuning also
extrapolates better to tables (for table-to-text) and
articles (for summarization) with unseen topics
(§6.4).
2 Related Work
Fine-tuning for natural language generation.
Current state-of-the-art systems for natural language generation are based on fine-tuning pretrained LMs. For table-to-text generation, Kale
(2020) fine-tunes a sequence-to-sequence model
(T5; Raffel et al., 2020). For extractive and abstractive summarization, researchers fine-tune masked
language models (e.g., BERT; Devlin et al., 2019)
and encode-decoder models (e.g., BART; Lewis
et al., 2020) respectively (Zhong et al., 2020; Liu
and Lapata, 2019; Raffel et al., 2020). For other
conditional NLG tasks such as machine translation and dialogue generation, fine-tuning is also the
prevalent paradigm (Zhang et al., 2020c; Stickland
et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020). In
this paper, we focus on table-to-text using GPT-2
and summarization using BART, but prefix-tuning
can be applied to other generation tasks and pretrained models.
Lightweight fine-tuning. Lightweight finetuning freezes most of the pretrained parameters
and modifies the pretrained model with small
trainable modules. The key challenge is to identify
high-performing architectures of the modules and
the subset of pretrained parameters to tune. One
line of research considers removing parameters:
some model weights are ablated away by training
a binary mask over model parameters (Zhao et al.,
2020; Radiya-Dixit and Wang, 2020). Another
line of research considers inserting parameters.
For example, Zhang et al. (2020a) trains a “side”
network that is fused with the pretrained model via
summation; adapter-tuning inserts task-specific layers (adapters) between each layer of the pretrained
LM (Houlsby et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2020; Rebuffi
et al., 2017; Pfeiffer et al., 2020). Compared to
this line of work, which tunes around 3.6% of the
LM parameters, our method obtains a further 30x
reduction in task-specific parameters, tuning only
0.1% while maintaining comparable performance.
Prompting. Prompting means prepending instructions and a few examples to the task input and
generating the output from the LM. GPT-3 (Brown
et al., 2020) uses manually designed prompts to
adapt its generation for different tasks, and this
framework is termed in-context learning. However,
since Transformers can only condition on a
bounded-length context (e.g., 2048 tokens for GPT3), in-context learning is unable to fully exploit
training sets longer than the context window. Sun
and Lai (2020) also prompt by keywords to control
for sentiment or topic of the generated sentence.
In natural language understanding tasks, prompt
engineering has been explored in prior works for
models like BERT and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019;
Jiang et al., 2020; Schick and Schutze ¨ , 2020). For
example, AutoPrompt (Shin et al., 2020) searches
for a sequence of discrete trigger words and concatenates it with each input to elicit sentiment or
factual knowledge from a masked LM. In contrast
with AutoPrompt, our method optimizes continuous prefixes, which are more expressive (§7.2);
moreover, we focus on language generation tasks.
Continuous vectors have been used to steer language models; for example, Subramani et al. (2020)
showed that a pretrained LSTM language model
can reconstruct arbitrary sentences by optimizing
a continuous vector for each sentence, making the
vector input-specific. In contrast, prefix-tuning optimizes a task-specific prefix that applies to all instances of that task. As a result, unlike the previous
work whose application is limited to sentence reconstruction, prefix-tuning can be applied to NLG
tasks.
Controllable generation. Controllable generation aims to steer a pretrained language model to
match a sentence level attribute (e.g., positive sentiment or topic on sports). Such control can happen
at training time: Keskar et al. (2019) pretrains the
language model (CTRL) to condition on metadata
such as keywords or URLs. Additionally, the control can happen at decoding time, by weighted decoding (GeDi, Krause et al., 2020) or iteratively updating the past activations (PPLM, Dathathri et al.,
2020). However, there is no straightforward way
to apply these controllable generation techniques
to enforce fine-grained control over generated contents, as demanded by tasks like table-to-text and
summarization.

4.1 Intuition
Based on intuition from prompting, we believe that
having a proper context can steer the LM without
changing its parameters. For example, if we want
the LM to generate a word (e.g., Obama), we can
prepend its common collocations as context (e.g.,
Barack), and the LM will assign much higher probability to the desired word. Extending this intuition
beyond generating a single word or sentence, we
want to find a context that steers the LM to solve
an NLG task. Intuitively, the context can influence the encoding of x by guiding what to extract
from x; and can influence the generation of y by
steering the next token distribution. However, it’s
non-obvious whether such a context exists. Natural
language task instructions (e.g., “summarize the
following table in one sentence”) might guide an
expert annotator to solve the task, but fail for most
pretrained LMs.2 Data-driven optimization over
the discrete instructions might help, but discrete
optimization is computationally challenging.
Instead of optimizing over discrete tokens, we
can optimize the instruction as continuous word embeddings, whose effects will be propagated upward
to all Transformer activation layers and rightward
to subsequent tokens. This is strictly more expressive than a discrete prompt which requires matching the embedding of a real word. Meanwhile,
this is less expressive than intervening all layers of
the activations (§7.2), which avoids long-range dependencies and includes more tunable parameters.
Prefix-tuning, therefore, optimizes all layers of the
prefix.

5 Experimental Setup
5.1 Datasets and Metrics
We evaluate on three standard neural generation
datasets for the table-to-text task: E2E (Novikova
et al., 2017), WebNLG (Gardent et al., 2017), and
DART (Radev et al., 2020). The datasets are ordered by increasing complexity and size. E2E only
has 1 domain (i.e. restaurant reviews); WebNLG
has 14 domains, and DART is open-domain, using
open-domain tables from Wikipedia.
The E2E dataset contains approximately 50K
examples with 8 distinct fields; it contains multiple
test references for one source table, and the average
output length is 22.9. We use the official evaluation
script, which reports BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002),
NIST (Belz and Reiter, 2006), METEOR (Lavie
and Agarwal, 2007), ROUGE-L (Lin, 2004), and
CIDEr (Vedantam et al., 2015).
The WebNLG (Gardent et al., 2017) dataset consists of 22K examples, and the input x is a sequence
of (subject, property, object) triples. The average
output length is 22.5. In the training and validation
splits, the input describes entities from 9 distinct
DBpedia categories (e.g., Monument). The test
split consists of two parts: the first half contains
DB categories seen in training data, and the second half contains 5 unseen categories. These unseen categories are used to evaluate extrapolation.
We use the official evaluation script, which reports
BLEU, METEOR and TER (Snover et al., 2006).
DART (Radev et al., 2020) is an open domain
table-to-text dataset, with similar input format
(entity-relation-entity triples) as WebNLG. The average output length is 21.6. It consists of 82K examples from WikiSQL, WikiTableQuestions, E2E,
and WebNLG and applies some manual or automated conversion. We use the official evaluation
script and report BLEU, METEOR, TER, MoverScore (Zhao et al., 2019), BERTScore (Zhang et al.,
2020b) and BLEURT (Sellam et al., 2020).
For the summarization task, we use the XSUM

6 Main Results
6.1 Table-to-text Generation
We find that adding only 0.1% task-specific parameters,9 prefix-tuning is effective in table-to-text generation, outperforming other lightweight baselines
(ADAPTER and FT-TOP2) and achieving a comparable performance with fine-tuning. This trend is
true across all three datasets: E2E, WebNLG,10 and
DART.
For a fair comparison, we match the number of
parameters for prefix-tuning and adapter-tuning to
be 0.1%. Table 1 shows that prefix-tuning is significantly better than ADAPTER (0.1%), attaining
4.1 BLEU improvement per dataset on average.
Even when we compare with fine-tuning (100%)
and adapter-tuning (3.0%), which update significantly more parameters than prefix-tuning, prefixtuning still achieves results comparable or better
than those two systems. This demonstrates that
prefix-tuning is more Pareto efficient than adaptertuning, significantly reducing parameters while improving generation quality.
Additionally, attaining good performance on
DART suggests that prefix-tuning can generalize
to tables with diverse domains and a large pool
of relations. We will delve deeper into extrapolation performance (i.e. generalization to unseen
categories or topics) in §6.4.
Overall, prefix-tuning is an effective and spaceefficient method to adapt GPT-2 to table-to-text
generation. The learned prefix is expressive enough
to steer GPT-2 in order to correctly extract contents
from an unnatural format and generate a textual
description. Prefix-tuning also scales well from
GPT-2MEDIUM to GPT-2LARGE, suggesting it has
the potential to scale to even larger models with a
similar architecture, like GPT-3.

7 Intrinsic Evaluation
We compare different variants of prefix-tuning.
§7.1 studies the impact of the prefix length. §7.2
studies tuning only the embedding layer, which is
more akin to tuning a discrete prompt. §7.3 compares prefixing and infixing, which inserts trainable
activations between x and y. §7.4 studies the impact of various prefix initialization strategies.
7.1 Prefix Length
A longer prefix means more trainable parameters,
and therefore more expressive power. Figure 4
shows that performance increases as the prefix
length increases up to a threshold (200 for summarization, 10 for table-to-text) and then a slight
performance drop occurs.14
Empirically, longer prefixes have a negligible
impact on inference speed, because attention computation over the entire prefix is parallellized on
GPUs.
7.2 Full vs Embedding-only
Recall in §4.1, we discuss the option of optimizing
the continuous embeddings of the “virtual tokens.”
We instantiate that idea and call it embedding-only
ablation. The word embeddings are free parameters, and the upper activation layers are computed
by the Transformer. Table 4 (top) shows that the
performance drops significantly, suggesting that
tuning only the embedding layer is not sufficiently
expressive.

7.3 Prefixing vs Infixing
We also investigate how the trainable activations’
position in the sequence affects performance. In
prefix-tuning, we place them at the beginning
[PREFIX; x; y]. We can also place the trainable
activations between x and y (i.e. [x; INFIX; y]) and
call this infix-tuning. Table 4 (bottom) shows that
infix-tuning slightly underperforms prefix-tuning.
We believe this is because prefix-tuning can affect
the activations of x and y whereas infix-tuning can
only influence the activations of y.
7.4 Initialization
We find that how the prefix is initialized has a large
impact in low-data settings. Random initialization
leads to low performance with high variance.
Initializing the prefix with activations of real words
significantly improves generation, as shown in Figure 5. In particular, initializing with task relevant
words such as “summarization” and “table-to-text”
obtains slightly better performance than task
irrelevant words such as “elephant” and “divide”,
but using real words is still better than random.
Since we initialize the prefix with activations
of real words computed by the LM, this initialization strategy is concordant with preserving the
pretrained LM as much as possible.
8 Discussion
In this section, we will discuss several favorable
properties of prefix-tuning and some open problems.
8.1 Personalization
As we note in §1, prefix-tuning is advantageous
when there are a large number of tasks that needs
to be trained independently. One practical setting is
user privacy (Shokri and Shmatikov, 2015; McMahan et al., 2016). In order to preserve user privacy,
each user’s data needs to be separated and a personalized model needs to be trained independently
for each user. Consequently, each user can be regarded as an independent task. If there are millions
of users, prefix-tuning can scale to this setting and
maintain modularity, enabling flexible addition or
deletion of users by adding or deleting their prefixes without cross-contamination.
8.2 Batching Across Users
Under the same personalization setting, prefixtuning allows batching different users’ queries even
though they are backed by different prefixes. When
multiple users query a cloud GPU device with their
inputs, it is computationally efficient to put these
users in the same batch. Prefix-tuning keeps the
shared LM intact; consequently, batching requires
a simple step of prepending the personalized prefix
to user input, and all the remaining computation
is unchanged. In contrast, we can’t batch across
different users in adapter-tuning, which has personalized adapters between shared Transformer layers.
8.3 Inductive Bias of Prefix-tuning
Recall that fine-tuning updates all pretrained parameters, whereas prefix-tuning and adapter-tuning
preserve them. Since the language models are pretrained on general purpose corpus, preserving the
LM parameters might help generalization to domains unseen during training. In concordance with
this intuition, we observe that both prefix-tuning
and adapter-tuning have significant performance
gain in extrapolation settings (§6.4); however, the
reason for such gain is an open question.
While prefix-tuning and adapter-tuning both
freeze the pretrained parameters, they tune different
sets of parameters to affect the activation layers of
the Transformer. Recall that prefix-tuning keeps the
LM intact and uses the prefix and the pretrained attention blocks to affect the subsequent activations;
adapter-tuning inserts trainable modules between
LM layers, which directly add residual vectors to
the activations. Moreover, we observe that prefixtuning requires vastly fewer parameters compared
to adapter-tuning while maintaining comparable
performance. We think this gain in parameter efficiency is because prefix-tuning keeps the pretrained
LM intact as much as possible, and therefore exploits the LM more than adapter-tuning.
Concurrent work by Aghajanyan et al. (2020)
uses intrinsic dimension to show that there exists
a low dimension reparameterization that is as effective for fine-tuning as the full parameter space.
This explains why good accuracy on downstream
task can be obtained by updating only a small number of parameters. Our work echoes the finding by
showing that good generation performance can be
attained by updating a very small prefix.
9 Conclusion
We have proposed prefix-tuning, a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning that prepends a trainable
continuous prefix for NLG tasks. We discover that
despite learning 1000x fewer parameters than finetuning, prefix-tuning can maintain a comparable
performance in a full data setting and outperforms
fine-tuning in both low-data and extrapolation settings.

Part 1. Petition Always Required
The following classifications always require a petition.
The initial evidence listed below and the initial evidence listed under the instructions for a change of status or extension of
stay must be included with a petition for a new or concurrent employment or for an extension where there is a change in
previously approved employment.
However, a petition for extension based on unchanged, previously approved employment should only be filed with the
initial evidence required in the extension of stay instructions.
E-2 CNMI
An E-2 CNMI investor is an alien who seeks to enter or remain in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana
Islands (CNMI) in order to maintain an investment in the CNMI that was approved by the CNMI government
prior to November 28, 2009. An E-2 CNMI investor classification is specifically limited to an alien investor who
has previously been granted a qualifying long term investor status under the laws of the CNMI. This classification
allows an eligible alien to be lawfully present in the CNMI in order to maintain the investment during the
transition period from CNMI to Federal immigration law. An investor’s nationality is not a qualifying factor in the
issuance of an E-2 CNMI investor classification.
This classification expires on December 31, 2029
A petition for the initial issuance of an E-2 CNMI investor classification must be filed within 2 years of the date the E-2
CNMI investor classification became available, which was January 18, 2011. Petitions for the initial issuance of the E-2
CNMI filed after January 18, 2013 will be rejected.
Requests for extension of the E-2 CNMI investor classification may be granted, in increments of not more than 2 years,
until December 31, 2029.
Applications for the dependents of E-2 CNMI investors must be filed on Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change
Nonimmigrant Status.
Write E-2C in the classification block.
The petition must be filed with documentary evidence of:
1. Continuous maintenance of the terms and conditions of E-2 CNMI investor nonimmigrant status;
2. Physical presence in the CNMI at the time of filing of the extension of stay request; and
3. The fact that the beneficiary will not leave during the pendency of the extension of stay request.

The H-1B classification is for aliens coming to the United States temporarily to perform services in a specialty
occupation.

A specialty occupation is one that requires the theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized
knowledge to fully perform the occupation and requires the attainment of a bachelor’s or higher degree in a specific
specialty, or its equivalent, as a minimum for entry into the occupation in the United States.
The petition must be filed by a U.S. employer or a U.S. agent and must be filed with:
1. Evidence that a labor condition application (LCA) has been certified by the U.S. Department of Labor;
2. Evidence showing that the proposed employment qualifies as a specialty occupation;
3. Evidence showing that the beneficiary has the required degree by submitting either:
A. A copy of the beneficiary’s U.S. bachelor’s or higher degree as required by the specialty occupation;
B. A copy of a foreign degree and evidence that it is equivalent to the U.S. degree; or
C. Evidence of education, specialized training, and/or progressively responsible experience that is equivalent to the
required U.S. degree.
4. A copy of any required license or other official permission to practice the occupation in the state of intended
employment; and
5. A copy of any written contract between the petitioner and the beneficiary or a summary of the terms of the oral
agreement under which the beneficiary will be employed.
6. If you are filing an H-1B cap petition for a fiscal year that H-1B registration is required, you must provide a valid
Beneficiary Confirmation Number for the beneficiary included in this petition, along with a copy of the H-1B
Registration Selection Notice.
NOTE: This evidence requirement is not applicable to H-1B2 petitions.
7. Off-site Assignment of H-1B Beneficiaries: Petitioners seeking to place the H-1B beneficiary off-site at a location
other than their own location must answer general questions regarding this assignment in Part 5., Basic Information
About the Proposed Employment and Employer. Petitioners should advise the H-1B beneficiary of the off-site

An H-1B cap-subject petition (including a petition eligible for the advanced degree exemption) only will be accepted for
filing if the underlying registration (or the petition itself, if the registration requirement is suspended) is selected toward
the annual numerical allocations. When applicable, registrations (or petitions) will be ranked and selected based on
the Occupational Employment Survey (OES) wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the
relevant Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code in their area(s) of intended employment. Therefore, in the
H-1B and H-1B1 Data Collection and Filing Fee Exemption Supplement, Item Number 11., you must specify the
highest OES wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage equals or exceeds for the relevant SOC code in the area(s)
of intended employment. The OES wage level selected in Part. 5, Item Number 11., must reflect the corresponding OES
wage level as of the date that the registration underlying the petition was submitted. However, if the registration process
is suspended, the OES wage level selected in Part. 5, Item Number 11., must reflect the corresponding OES wage level
as of the date that the petition is filed.
The proffered wage is the wage that you intend to pay the beneficiary as indicated on the petition. The SOC code and
area(s) of intended employment should be indicated on the LCA filed with the petition.
NOTE: If the beneficiary will work in multiple locations, or in multiple positions if you are filing the petition as an agent,
you must select the lowest corresponding OES wage level that the proffered wage will equal or exceed. If the proffered
wage is expressed as a range, you must select the OES wage level based on the lowest wage in the range. If you are
relying on a prevailing wage that is not based on the OES survey, and the proffered wage is less than the corresponding
level I OES wage, you must select the “Wage Level I and below” box. You may not lower the proffered wage listed on the
petition to an amount that would be equivalent to a lower wage level than the wage level reflected on the selected H-1B
registration. If the relevant SOC code does not have current OES prevailing wage information available, you should
follow U.S. Department of Labor guidance on prevailing wage determinations to determine which OES wage level to
select.
